LESSON 73 OF 106·Social Engineering and the Human Factor

Vishing, Smishing and Quishing

Why the channel changed but the attack did not: voice, SMS and QR codes, why caller ID can be spoofed, and the one mobile habit that works everywhere.

Foundation14 min
Why this matters

The same social engineering works over voice, text and QR codes. Each channel has its own weaknesses, and each exploits something different about how people behave in that medium.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

Architecture & Trust Boundary Flow

Interactive mental model for Vishing, Smishing and Quishing: compare normal operation, boundary failure, and defensive design.

  1. Vector: An attacker or faulty client alters parameters, headers, timing, or sequence order.

01 Untrusted Input

  1. Verification: Publish one verified number for the service desk, and instruct staff to call back on it rather than accept an incoming call.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.
  3. Resilience: Invalid requests fail closed and emit structured security telemetry.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Voice works because it creates real time pressure and because the caller can react to what the target says.
  • A caller who already knows internal terminology, a name or a project detail has credibility immediately.
  • Text is limited in length, which pushes attackers to use brevity and a single clear instruction.
  • A QR code moves the target to a physical-looking action, which bypasses the habit of reading a URL before visiting it.
  • The common thread is a request to change channel, break process, or act before verifying.

The background

  • Cold-calling support desks was an early and effective technique, and largely stopped once verification improved.
  • Voice phishing returned with the availability of caller identity spoofing and cheap international calling.
  • Text messaging gained traction once business communication moved to phones.
  • QR codes created a new delivery channel precisely because scanning does not involve reading an address.

Real-world examples

  • A caller claiming to be from the service desk, already knowing the employee name, is routinely convincing.
  • A message about a failed delivery is expected, so a link in it is not surprising.
  • A code of conduct or parking notice placed in a car park is a genuine lure rather than a mistake.

What to look for

  • Check whether the caller already knows things they should not, and treat internal knowledge as suspicious rather than reassuring.
  • Check whether the request moves to another channel, which is the point where the original trust stops applying.
  • Check whether you are being asked to bypass a process, especially for a supposedly urgent account issue.
  • Check whether the message arrives on a channel you did not expect to hear from that person on.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Multifactor Authentication

Reading why a second factor changes the economics of a phishing attack, and which kinds of second factor resist a relayed or copied credential

Open CISA resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Publish one verified number for the service desk, and instruct staff to call back on it rather than accept an incoming call.
  • Never ask for a one-time code, password or remote access in response to an unsolicited contact.
  • Verify payment or credential changes through a channel the requester did not initiate.
  • Treat an unexpected code of conduct or payment request as a reportable event, not a minor irritation.
  • Practise the call-back habit explicitly, because it is the control that works across every channel.
